doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

title: Starting on trombone, Henry Street Settlement and Howard Saposnik's junior high band
summary: Band class, scholarship at Henry Street Settlement, and the band director who moved him to tuba.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Were you attracted to the bass clef at that point? I’m trying to figure out what brought you to the tuba.

My evolution into the tuba is that when I was very young, in elementary school they started a band program in my elementary school. And I brought the notice home to my mother and she was very excited. And so she signed me up for it, and I started, you know, so in those days you started as a class. You started as a band class. I started in the band class where you have clarinets, trumpets, trombones and everything in the class. Everybody learned at the same time. It’s not like I went out for a private instruction lesson. So everybody learned at the same time. So in those days what they did was they determined maybe your arm length, your lip size, and your body size to determine what instrument they choose so they can balance out the band. So he thought my arms were long enough to be able to manipulate a trombone, and my lips were a good size, they could, you know, really fit into a trombone mouthpiece. So my initial band director started me on the trombone, which I like tremendously. And then my mother, she really wanted me to excel so down on the lower east side of Manhattan there was a historical music school called the Henry Street Settlement. It’s been there for decades and everything. And they offered scholarships. So my mother brought me down and filled out the scholarship forms and they gave me — just based on financial need and everything. So I got a scholarship to study theory and trombone. And so because of that I began to excel and I became a really fine trombone player by the time I got through junior high school. And the junior high school band I entered into, the band director was Howard Saposnik. And he had a band in junior high school of a hundred pieces of every

instrument: bassoons, trombones, trumpets, tubas you name it. Full clarinet section. And he played trumpet himself and then every day he’d have the band play [scats]. And the way he got us to want to do that is one of the first lessons he did, he would just take out the trumpet. He went [scats]. And that sounded so good that everybody wanted to be able to do it. So every rehearsal we’d start, right through the keys. He would have a different key. So we’d go like through all twelve keys. By the end of the year we got through [scats], and then the chromatic scale [scats]. So you know it was a tremendous, tremendous band mainly because of the director and the inspiration. So he really inspired me. So I became a really fine — I was playing first trombone and he came over to me one day and he says, “Listen, you know, you’re a really really fine trombonist and I need somebody to move into the tuba section because we’re short there. We’re slightly off balance and we need to add another tuba into the section.” So you know you could imagine the admiration I had for this man, his brilliant playing and his brilliant way of teaching a class, so anything that he would say — I would have probably done it. So anyway I said sure you know. So I put the trombone down and he brought me in for a couple of days, just to get me oriented with the tuba and everything. And then I just took to it. It just became a natural thing. I just took to it. And the tuba became my voice at a very, very early age. And I just progressed so fast that within a month or so he was able to place me, in New York at that time they had borough-wide bands where the best students from all the boroughs would go, like Manhattan had theirs, Queens had theirs, you know, the Bronx had theirs. So I was placed into the Manhattan borough-wide band. And I did exceptionally well there in the band. And I progressed until they moved me into the orchestra. The orchestra was for really select brass players. Because the orchestra, you know, mainly the orchestra would just work with strings and then they would bring the brass and the woodwinds in towards the end. So you’d have to be a good reader.
